questions.q: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, with T(1) = 1, solves to
questions.e: Here a = 2, b = 2, so n^(log_b a) = n, which equals f(n) = n. Case 2 of the master theorem gives Θ(n log n), as in merge sort.

questions.q: The fractional knapsack problem is solved optimally by a greedy method that picks items in decreasing order of
questions.e: Taking the item with the best value per unit weight first is optimal when fractions are allowed. This greedy rule fails for the 0/1 knapsack.

questions.q: At every step of Huffman's algorithm, the two nodes that are merged are those with the ______ frequencies.
questions.e: Merging the two least frequent nodes pushes rare symbols deeper in the tree, giving them longer codes and minimising the weighted code length.

questions.q: The Floyd–Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths on a graph with V vertices runs in time
questions.e: It has three nested loops over k, i and j, each running V times.

questions.q: Which of the following problems is NOT typically solved by backtracking?
questions.e: Huffman coding is built greedily by repeatedly merging the two least frequent nodes. N-queens, graph colouring and Hamiltonian cycle are solved by extending partial solutions and backtracking when they fail.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Every problem in P is also in NP.
II. Every problem in NP is NP-complete.
Which of the above is/are correct?
questions.e: A problem solvable in polynomial time is certainly verifiable in polynomial time, so P ⊆ NP. NP also contains easy problems such as sorting, which are not NP-complete.

questions.q: The dynamic programming solution for the longest common subsequence of strings of lengths m and n takes time
questions.e: The table has (m + 1)(n + 1) entries and each is filled in constant time from three neighbours.

questions.q:
Let f(n) = 3n² + 5n + 7. Consider the following statements.
I. f(n) = O(n).
II. f(n) = Ω(n³).
Which of the above is/are correct?
questions.e: The dominant term is 3n², so f(n) = Θ(n²). It grows faster than n, so it is not O(n), and slower than n³, so it is not Ω(n³). Both statements are false.

questions.q: Dijkstra's single-source shortest path algorithm can produce wrong results if the graph contains
questions.e: Once a vertex is extracted its distance is treated as final, which is valid only if no later path can be shorter. A negative edge can break this.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
questions.e: Kruskal's algorithm is greedy: it keeps adding the cheapest edge that creates no cycle. Merge sort, quick sort and Strassen's method split the problem into subproblems, solve them and combine the results.

questions.q:
Consider the following recurrences.
I. T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² solves to Θ(n² log n).
II. T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n solves to Θ(n²).
Which of the above is/are correct?
questions.e: Here a = 4 and b = 2, so n^(log₂4) = n². In I, f(n) = n² matches it, giving Θ(n² log n). In II, f(n) = n grows more slowly, so the leaves dominate and T(n) = Θ(n²). Both are true.

questions.q: Five symbols have frequencies 3, 5, 7, 10 and 15. The total weighted code length (sum of frequency × code length) in an optimal Huffman code is
questions.e: Merges: 3+5=8, 7+8=15, 10+15=25, 15+25=40. The weighted length equals the sum of the merged weights: 8 + 15 + 25 + 40 = 88.

questions.q: A knapsack of capacity 40 is to be filled from four divisible items with (value, weight) = (60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30) and (30, 5). The maximum total value is
questions.e: Ratios are 6, 5, 4 and 6. Take (60, 10) and (30, 5), then (100, 20): weight 35 and value 190. The remaining 5 units of the last item add 120 × 5/30 = 20, giving 210.

questions.q: A 0/1 knapsack has capacity 10 and items with (value, weight) = (10, 5), (40, 4), (30, 6) and (50, 3). The maximum value obtainable is
questions.e: The best fit is the items worth 40 and 50, with total weight 7 and value 90. Adding any other item exceeds 10. The set worth 100 would weigh 12, which is infeasible.

questions.q: Matrices A (10 × 20), B (20 × 5) and C (5 × 30) are to be multiplied. The minimum number of scalar multiplications needed is
The length of a longest common subsequence of the strings BCDBCA and ABCBDAB is
questions.e: One common subsequence of length 4 is BCBA (B-C-B-A appears in order in both strings). No common subsequence of length 5 exists, as the DP table confirms.

questions.q: An undirected graph has vertices 0 to 7 and edges 0–1, 1–2, 2–0, 1–3, 3–4, 4–5, 5–3, 4–6 and 6–7. Its articulation points are
questions.e: Removing 1 cuts off {0, 2}, removing 3 cuts off {0, 1, 2}, removing 4 cuts off {6, 7}, and removing 6 cuts off 7. Vertices 0, 2 and 5 lie in triangles, and 7 is a leaf, so none of them is one.

questions.q: How many subsets of the set {3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10} have elements adding up to exactly 15?
questions.e: The subsets are {5, 10}, {7, 8} and {3, 5, 7}. A subset containing 6 would need 9 from {3, 5, 7, 8, 10}, which is impossible, and {3, 5, 7} is the only 3-element case.

questions.q: A directed graph on vertices 1 to 4 has edges 1→2 (3), 1→4 (7), 2→1 (8), 2→3 (2), 3→1 (5), 3→4 (1) and 4→1 (2). In the Floyd–Warshall algorithm, after the iteration for k = 2 is complete (paths may use vertices 1 and 2 as intermediates), the entry d[2][4] is
questions.e: Before any better route is allowed, 2→4 can go only through 1: 2→1→4 = 8 + 7 = 15. The cheaper route 2→3→4 = 3 needs vertex 3 as intermediate and appears only at k = 3.

questions.q: The recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/4) + n, with T(1) = 1, has the solution
questions.e: The master theorem does not apply. At each level of the recursion tree the total work shrinks by a factor of (1/2 + 1/4) = 3/4, so the sum is a geometric series bounded by 4n, which is Θ(n).
